description: 100 PvP-ready defensive social-engineering questions for LevelBlue.

question_types.description: Fast four-choice social-engineering scenarios designed for LevelBlue PvP.

scenario.subject: URGENT: Account expires today
scenario.body: Your student account will be deleted in 30 minutes. Sign in using the link below to keep access.

questions.question: What is the safest action?
options: Open the official school portal separately and verify the alert.
Reply with your password to confirm ownership.
Click the link before the timer expires.
Forward the message to classmates and ask if it is real.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Urgency plus a non-school sender domain are warning signs. Verify through an official channel instead of using the message link.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Urgency plus a non-school sender domain are warning signs. Verify through an official channel instead of using the message link.
questions.explanation: Urgency plus a non-school sender domain are warning signs. Verify through an official channel instead of using the message link.

scenario.subject: Enrollment schedule
scenario.body: Enrollment for next term opens Monday. Visit the normal student portal when registration begins. No reply is required.

questions.question: Which detail most strongly suggests this message may be legitimate?
options: The sender used a formal greeting.
It uses the expected school domain and does not ask for credentials.
It mentions enrollment.
It arrived during school hours.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — A known domain and the absence of credential requests or urgent links are stronger trust signals than tone or timing.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. A known domain and the absence of credential requests or urgent links are stronger trust signals than tone or timing.
questions.explanation: A known domain and the absence of credential requests or urgent links are stronger trust signals than tone or timing.

scenario.subject: Password check required
scenario.body: We detected an error. Reply with your username and password so IT can test your account.

questions.question: What is the clearest red flag?
options: The sender uses the word 'error'.
The message is short.
The subject mentions IT.
The message asks you to send your password.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Legitimate support staff should not ask you to send your password by email.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Legitimate support staff should not ask you to send your password by email.
questions.explanation: Legitimate support staff should not ask you to send your password by email.

scenario.subject: Overdue book reminder
scenario.body: You have an overdue library book. Check your account through the library page you normally use.

questions.question: What should you do before acting?
options: Reply with your student password.
Send your ID number to the sender.
Ignore every library message.
Navigate to the known library site yourself instead of using unexpected links.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Using a known site or bookmark reduces the risk of following a spoofed link.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Using a known site or bookmark reduces the risk of following a spoofed link.
questions.explanation: Using a known site or bookmark reduces the risk of following a spoofed link.

scenario.subject: You have been selected!
scenario.body: Claim your scholarship today by entering your school login and bank details.

questions.question: Which social-engineering tactic is being used most clearly?
options: The attacker is physically tailgating.
The attacker is encrypting your files.
A tempting reward is being used to pressure you into revealing information.
The attacker is shoulder surfing.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Unexpected rewards are commonly used as bait, especially when the message asks for sensitive information.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Unexpected rewards are commonly used as bait, especially when the message asks for sensitive information.
questions.explanation: Unexpected rewards are commonly used as bait, especially when the message asks for sensitive information.

scenario.subject: Mia shared a document
scenario.body: Open the shared document and sign in with your school account to view it.

questions.question: What should you check first?
options: Whether the document title sounds interesting.
Whether the message has a logo.
Whether the sharing notification came from the real document service domain.
Whether your friend usually sends homework.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Branding can be copied. The actual sender domain and destination are more useful checks.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Branding can be copied. The actual sender domain and destination are more useful checks.
questions.explanation: Branding can be copied. The actual sender domain and destination are more useful checks.

scenario.subject: Need a quick favor
scenario.body: I am in a meeting. Buy four gift cards and email me the codes immediately.

questions.question: What is the best response?
options: Send the codes but keep the receipts.
Reply asking which gift-card brand to buy.
Verify the request through a known school contact method.
Buy one card first to test the request.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Gift-card requests combined with urgency and secrecy are common impersonation scams.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Gift-card requests combined with urgency and secrecy are common impersonation scams.
questions.explanation: Gift-card requests combined with urgency and secrecy are common impersonation scams.

scenario.subject: Unusual sign-in
scenario.body: We blocked a sign-in. Review activity at https://micros0ft-login.com/security.

questions.question: Which detail is the strongest technical clue?
options: The domain uses a lookalike spelling with a zero instead of the letter o.
The link begins with https.
The email contains a company name.
The message mentions security.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — HTTPS does not prove a site is legitimate. Lookalike domains are a common phishing indicator.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. HTTPS does not prove a site is legitimate. Lookalike domains are a common phishing indicator.
questions.explanation: HTTPS does not prove a site is legitimate. Lookalike domains are a common phishing indicator.

scenario.subject: Updated reimbursement form
scenario.body: Please review the attached spreadsheet and enable editing to see the payment information.

questions.question: What should you do?
options: Enable editing because the sender domain looks correct.
Disable antivirus temporarily so the file opens.
Confirm the attachment through a trusted channel before opening or enabling content.
Upload the file to a public website for checking.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Even apparently trusted accounts can be compromised. Unexpected active-content attachments should be independently verified.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Even apparently trusted accounts can be compromised. Unexpected active-content attachments should be independently verified.
questions.explanation: Even apparently trusted accounts can be compromised. Unexpected active-content attachments should be independently verified.

scenario.subject: Password reset requested
scenario.body: A password reset was requested for your account. If this was not you, open the school portal directly and review security settings.

questions.question: You did not request a reset. What is the best next step?
options: Use the official portal directly and secure the account.
Ignore the event permanently.
Reply to the email with your old password.
Click every link in the message to inspect them.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — An unexpected reset can indicate attempted account access. Use a known official route, not an embedded link.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. An unexpected reset can indicate attempted account access. Use a known official route, not an embedded link.
questions.explanation: An unexpected reset can indicate attempted account access. Use a known official route, not an embedded link.

scenario.subject: Confidential student list
scenario.body: Send me the class roster with student phone numbers right now. Do not copy anyone else.

questions.question: Why should you verify this request even if the address looks correct?
options: Confidential requests are always fake.
The account could be compromised and the request involves sensitive data.
Phone numbers are never considered personal information.
School addresses can never send attachments.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — A familiar account is not proof of authenticity. Unusual requests for sensitive information deserve independent verification.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. A familiar account is not proof of authenticity. Unusual requests for sensitive information deserve independent verification.
questions.explanation: A familiar account is not proof of authenticity. Unusual requests for sensitive information deserve independent verification.

scenario.subject: Bank update
scenario.body: Your allowance deposit failed. Sign in here and re-enter your bank details before 3 PM.

questions.question: Which combination is most suspicious?
options: A short subject and formal wording.
An unfamiliar domain, financial information request, and urgent deadline.
The message was sent before 3 PM.
The message mentions payroll and banking.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Multiple red flags together increase the likelihood of phishing.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Multiple red flags together increase the likelihood of phishing.
questions.explanation: Multiple red flags together increase the likelihood of phishing.

scenario.subject: Re: Poster draft
scenario.body: Here is the updated draft. Download Poster_Final.zip and run the included viewer to open it.

questions.question: What is the safest response?
options: Confirm with the teammate through another channel before running the file.
Rename the file extension before opening.
Turn off file warnings so it opens faster.
Run it because it is part of an existing thread.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Attackers can hijack real threads or accounts. Executable or unusual files should be verified.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Attackers can hijack real threads or accounts. Executable or unusual files should be verified.
questions.explanation: Attackers can hijack real threads or accounts. Executable or unusual files should be verified.

scenario.subject: MFA synchronization
scenario.body: Reply with the six-digit code sent to your phone so we can resync your account.

questions.question: What should you do?
options: Approve any login prompt that appears.
Send only the first three digits.
Send the code because it expires quickly.
Never share the one-time code and contact the help desk through its official number.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — One-time authentication codes are secrets and can be used to take over accounts.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. One-time authentication codes are secrets and can be used to take over accounts.
questions.explanation: One-time authentication codes are secrets and can be used to take over accounts.

scenario.subject: Receipt available
scenario.body: Your receipt is ready. The message contains a button labeled VIEW RECEIPT.

questions.question: Before clicking, what is the most useful check?
options: Inspect the actual destination and confirm it belongs to the expected service.
Check whether the sender used your first name.
Check whether the button is blue.
Check whether the email has the school logo.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Visual design and personalization are easy to fake; destination domains matter more.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Visual design and personalization are easy to fake; destination domains matter more.
questions.explanation: Visual design and personalization are easy to fake; destination domains matter more.

scenario.subject: Re: Group grades
scenario.body: Can you send me the verification code that just appeared on your phone? I am fixing the grade portal.

questions.question: What makes this dangerous even though it comes from the real teacher account?
options: School accounts cannot be compromised.
The teacher's account may be compromised and a verification code should not be shared.
Teachers are not allowed to send email.
Verification codes are safe if the requester knows you.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Compromised trusted accounts are powerful phishing tools. Never share authentication codes.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Compromised trusted accounts are powerful phishing tools. Never share authentication codes.
questions.explanation: Compromised trusted accounts are powerful phishing tools. Never share authentication codes.

scenario.subject: RE: October invoice
scenario.body: Our bank account changed. Use the new account in the attached instructions for today's payment.

questions.question: What is the safest verification method?
options: Send a small payment first.
Use the phone number printed in the attachment.
Call the vendor using a previously known phone number, not contact details in the email.
Reply to the same email asking for confirmation.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Payment-change fraud is best verified through a trusted contact path established before the suspicious message.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Payment-change fraud is best verified through a trusted contact path established before the suspicious message.
questions.explanation: Payment-change fraud is best verified through a trusted contact path established before the suspicious message.

scenario.subject: Incident response
scenario.body: We found malware on your account. Open the attached remote-support tool and send the session code to this email.

questions.question: What is the key risk?
options: Session codes are public information.
Security teams never contact users.
The message is trying to make you install or grant remote access without independent verification.
Remote-support tools are always malware.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Legitimate remote support should be initiated and verified through approved support procedures.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Legitimate remote support should be initiated and verified through approved support procedures.
questions.explanation: Legitimate remote support should be initiated and verified through approved support procedures.

scenario.subject: Re: Notes
scenario.body: I uploaded the notes here: westfield.edu.notes-share.co/login. Sign in with your school account.

questions.question: Which domain actually controls the site?
options: edu.notes-share
westfield.edu
notes-share.co
login
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — The registrable domain is notes-share.co; 'westfield.edu' appears only as a subdomain-like label intended to mislead.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. The registrable domain is notes-share.co; 'westfield.edu' appears only as a subdomain-like label intended to mislead.
questions.explanation: The registrable domain is notes-share.co; 'westfield.edu' appears only as a subdomain-like label intended to mislead.

scenario.subject: New device sign-in
scenario.body: You receive a convincing alert after accidentally entering your password on a suspicious page five minutes earlier.

questions.question: What should you do first?
options: Change the password through the official site and review active sessions/MFA.
Reuse the same password on another account.
Reply to the suspicious page and ask it to delete your password.
Wait to see whether anything happens.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — After suspected credential exposure, use the official service to change credentials and review account security immediately.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. After suspected credential exposure, use the official service to change credentials and review account security immediately.
questions.explanation: After suspected credential exposure, use the official service to change credentials and review account security immediately.

scenario.body: Classes are suspended tomorrow. Check the official school page for the full announcement.

questions.question: Which action is safest?
options: Tap any shortened link you receive afterward.
Reply with your password to confirm you are a student.
Send your student ID to the number.
Open the school's known website or official channel yourself.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — When a message can be verified through an official public channel, use that route.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. When a message can be verified through an official public channel, use that route.

scenario.body: You won a new phone! Claim it now: prize-now.example

questions.question: What social-engineering trigger is being used?
options: Authority only.
Physical intimidation.
A reward or prize.
Encryption.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Unexpected prizes are designed to create excitement and reduce careful checking.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Unexpected prizes are designed to create excitement and reduce careful checking.

scenario.body: My phone broke. This is my new number. I need money urgently for transport.

questions.question: What should you do first?
options: Contact the family member using a previously known number or another trusted method.
Send a small amount first.
Save the new number and trust it.
Ask for their bank account immediately.

questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Family-emergency impersonation should be verified independently before sending money or information.
questions.explanation: Family-emergency impersonation should be verified independently before sending money or information.

scenario.body: Your login code is 482193. Do not share this code with anyone.

questions.question: Someone immediately texts asking you to send them the code. What should you do?
options: Do not share the code.
Post it in the group chat to ask if it is safe.
Send only the last three digits.
Send it if they claim to be support.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — One-time passwords are authentication secrets.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. One-time passwords are authentication secrets.

scenario.body: Hi, is this Carla? Sorry, wrong number! By the way, what school do you attend?

questions.question: What is the safest response?
options: Answer so they know they reached a real person.
Tell them your school but not your name.
Send your social-media profile instead.
Avoid sharing personal details with the unknown sender.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Wrong-number conversations can be used to collect personal information or build trust.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Wrong-number conversations can be used to collect personal information or build trust.
questions.explanation: Wrong-number conversations can be used to collect personal information or build trust.

scenario.body: We detected a virus. Install the security app from this link now: bit.ly/secure-campus

options: Install it because the message says IT.
Contact campus IT through its official support channel before installing anything.
Send the link to classmates.
Disable phone security before installing.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Unexpected software-install requests should be independently verified.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Unexpected software-install requests should be independently verified.
questions.explanation: Unexpected software-install requests should be independently verified.

scenario.body: FINAL NOTICE: Unpaid road fee. Pay PHP 75 today to avoid a PHP 3,000 penalty: toll-pay.example

questions.question: Which tactic is most obvious?
options: The attacker is asking for a physical key.
The attacker is shoulder surfing.
The attacker is offering technical support.
A small immediate payment is paired with a large threatened penalty.

questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Threats and disproportionate penalties create pressure to act quickly.
questions.explanation: Threats and disproportionate penalties create pressure to act quickly.

scenario.body: We saw your profile. Earn PHP 5,000 per day. Pay a PHP 300 verification fee to begin.

questions.question: What is the best assessment?
options: Send an ID photo before asking questions.
Share the offer publicly to prove it is real.
Pay because the salary is high.
Treat it as suspicious because legitimate hiring should not require an unexpected upfront verification payment.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — High-reward job offers combined with upfront fees are a common social-engineering lure.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. High-reward job offers combined with upfront fees are a common social-engineering lure.
questions.explanation: High-reward job offers combined with upfront fees are a common social-engineering lure.

scenario.body: Vote for me in this contest! Log in with your school account here: vote-campus.example

questions.question: You know the sender. Why should you still be careful?
options: Their messaging account could be compromised.
School accounts are never used for voting.
Friends cannot send links.
Voting websites are always fake.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Compromised accounts often spread malicious links through trusted contacts.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Compromised accounts often spread malicious links through trusted contacts.
questions.explanation: Compromised accounts often spread malicious links through trusted contacts.

scenario.body: We will call you next. When the call arrives, read us the code we just sent to verify your identity.

options: Delete the code and approve the next login.
Send a screenshot of the code instead.
Share it only during the call.
Do not share the code; contact the bank through its official number.

questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Attackers may combine texts and calls to capture authentication codes.
questions.explanation: Attackers may combine texts and calls to capture authentication codes.

scenario.body: Your package address is incomplete. Reply with your full name, home address, birth date, and school ID number.

questions.question: What is the biggest concern?
options: The message requests far more personal information than is necessary for delivery.
Addresses are never needed for delivery.
Delivery services cannot send texts.
Birth dates are public information.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Excessive data requests are a strong warning sign.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Excessive data requests are a strong warning sign.
questions.explanation: Excessive data requests are a strong warning sign.

scenario.body: Your account was charged PHP 8,900. If this was not you, call 09XX-XXX-XXXX immediately.

options: Call the number in the message immediately.
Send the text your account number.
Reply 'NO' with your PIN.
Use the number on your bank card or official banking app instead of the number in the text.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — A scam text may direct victims to an attacker-controlled phone number.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. A scam text may direct victims to an attacker-controlled phone number.
questions.explanation: A scam text may direct victims to an attacker-controlled phone number.

scenario.body: Security warning: Your account will be removed for copyright violations. Appeal at social-appeal.example.

options: Open the social platform directly and check account notifications there.
Reply with your password.
Appeal through the text link before deletion.
Ask the sender to extend the deadline.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Use the service's official app or website to verify threatening account notices.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Use the service's official app or website to verify threatening account notices.
questions.explanation: Use the service's official app or website to verify threatening account notices.

scenario.body: Can you vote for my project? I need your phone number first so the site can send you a voting code. Then send me the code.

questions.question: What is likely happening?
options: The sender may be trying to use your verification code to access an account.
The code is only for voting and is safe.
The sender needs the code to prove friendship.
Voting codes cannot be used for authentication.

questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Requests to relay verification codes are a common account-takeover technique.
questions.explanation: Requests to relay verification codes are a common account-takeover technique.

scenario.body: Security: A new eSIM was requested for your number. Reply YES to cancel.

options: Carriers never send security alerts.

questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Security alerts should be verified through a trusted carrier channel rather than instructions in an unexpected message.
questions.explanation: Security alerts should be verified through a trusted carrier channel rather than instructions in an unexpected message.

scenario.body: I'm in a client meeting. Buy digital gift cards and send the codes here. Keep this confidential.

options: New number, urgency, secrecy, and an unusual payment request.
The boss is in a meeting.
Gift cards can be bought online.
The request is sent by text.

questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Multiple social-engineering pressure signals appearing together are a strong warning.
questions.explanation: Multiple social-engineering pressure signals appearing together are a strong warning.

scenario.body: Campus emergency. Confirm your safety and location at westfield.edu.safety-check.example.

The '.edu' text anywhere in the address.

questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Attackers can place trusted names earlier in a hostname. The actual registrable domain matters.

scenario.body: The caller asks you to install remote-support software and read a session code.

questions.question: What should you do?
options: End the call and start a support session only through the official IT process.
Give the session code but not your password.
Turn off antivirus first.
Install it because remote support is normal.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Remote access is powerful and should be initiated only through a trusted support workflow.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Remote access is powerful and should be initiated only through a trusted support workflow.
questions.explanation: Remote access is powerful and should be initiated only through a trusted support workflow.

scenario.body: The caller says the principal urgently needs student contact lists for an 'inspection.'

questions.question: What is the safest response?
options: Ask the caller to say the principal's first name.
Read the list aloud instead of emailing it.
Send the list because the request comes from authority.
Verify the request with the office through a known internal contact method.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Authority claims do not replace verification when sensitive data is involved.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Authority claims do not replace verification when sensitive data is involved.
questions.explanation: Authority claims do not replace verification when sensitive data is involved.

scenario.body: A caller asks, 'Can you hear me?' and then begins requesting account information.

questions.question: What should guide your response?
options: Do not disclose sensitive information; verify the caller's identity and purpose independently.
Say yes repeatedly to prove the line works.
Trust the call if the connection is clear.
Give basic account details before asking questions.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — The core risk is disclosure to an unverified caller, not a particular opening phrase.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. The core risk is disclosure to an unverified caller, not a particular opening phrase.
questions.explanation: The core risk is disclosure to an unverified caller, not a particular opening phrase.

scenario.body: The caller says your SIM will be disabled unless you read them a one-time code.

questions.question: What should you do?
options: Do not share the code; contact the carrier using its official app or number.
Send a screenshot instead of reading it.
Share the code because SIM issues are urgent.
Ask the caller to text the code back to you.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Authentication codes can authorize sensitive account changes such as SIM transfers.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Authentication codes can authorize sensitive account changes such as SIM transfers.
questions.explanation: Authentication codes can authorize sensitive account changes such as SIM transfers.

scenario.body: A vendor calls asking you to change payment details immediately and emails new bank information during the call.

questions.question: What is the safest verification?
options: Trust the caller because they also emailed.
Make a small test transfer.
Use a previously known vendor contact to confirm the change.
Use the phone number in the new email.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Independent verification through an established contact path protects against impersonation.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Independent verification through an established contact path protects against impersonation.
questions.explanation: Independent verification through an established contact path protects against impersonation.

scenario.body: A caller correctly describes a recent school event, then asks for your login.

questions.question: Why is the background knowledge not enough to trust them?
options: Security staff never know school events.
Only students can see public information.
Public information can be used to make a false story sound credible.
Knowing an event means the caller is an employee.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Pretexting often combines publicly available facts with impersonation.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Pretexting often combines publicly available facts with impersonation.
questions.explanation: Pretexting often combines publicly available facts with impersonation.

scenario.body: The caller pressures you to stay on the line while moving money to a 'safe account.'

questions.question: What should you do?
options: Move a small amount first.
Stay on the line but refuse to answer questions.
Hang up and contact the bank through its official channel.
Ask the caller to send the safe-account number by text.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Banks do not protect money by asking customers to transfer it to an unknown 'safe' account.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Banks do not protect money by asking customers to transfer it to an unknown 'safe' account.
questions.explanation: Banks do not protect money by asking customers to transfer it to an unknown 'safe' account.

scenario.body: The voice sounds exactly like your teacher and asks for an MFA code to fix the class portal.

questions.question: What is the safest assumption?
options: A familiar voice proves identity.
MFA codes are safe to share with teachers.
An AI-generated voice cannot sound convincing.
Voice alone is not proof; verify through an established school channel.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Voice cloning makes voice recognition alone an unreliable authentication method.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Voice cloning makes voice recognition alone an unreliable authentication method.
questions.explanation: Voice cloning makes voice recognition alone an unreliable authentication method.

scenario.body: A caller appears to be calling from a real internal extension and requests confidential records.

questions.question: Why should you still verify?
options: Internal numbers are never real.
Caller ID and internal numbers can be spoofed or accounts can be compromised.
Only external calls can be fraudulent.
Confidential records can always be shared internally.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Technical indicators such as caller ID are not sufficient proof of identity.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Technical indicators such as caller ID are not sufficient proof of identity.
questions.explanation: Technical indicators such as caller ID are not sufficient proof of identity.

scenario.body: You receive repeated MFA prompts. Seconds later, 'IT' calls and says approving one will stop the alerts.

questions.question: What attack pattern does this resemble?
options: Physical tailgating.
Shoulder surfing.
MFA fatigue combined with impersonation.
Dumpster diving.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Attackers may flood a user with prompts and then impersonate support to convince them to approve one.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Attackers may flood a user with prompts and then impersonate support to convince them to approve one.
questions.explanation: Attackers may flood a user with prompts and then impersonate support to convince them to approve one.

scenario.body: The caller orders an urgent confidential payment and says normal approval steps can be skipped because of an emergency.

questions.question: What is the correct response?
options: Ask a coworker whether the caller sounded confident.
Follow the established payment-verification process despite the claimed emergency.
Send half the payment first.
Skip controls because a director outranks them.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Social engineering often exploits authority and urgency to bypass established controls.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Social engineering often exploits authority and urgency to bypass established controls.
questions.explanation: Social engineering often exploits authority and urgency to bypass established controls.

scenario.body: The caller asks you to read information displayed in your authenticator app, including login location and number-matching details.

questions.question: What should you do?
options: Keep retrying until the prompt disappears.
Share the location but not the number.
Approve if the caller knows your username.
Do not approve or disclose authentication details for a login you did not initiate.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Authentication prompts should correspond to actions you personally initiated.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Authentication prompts should correspond to actions you personally initiated.
questions.explanation: Authentication prompts should correspond to actions you personally initiated.

question_types.description: Fast four-choice social-engineering scenarios designed for LevelBlue PvP.

scenario.body: A person says they forgot their badge and asks you to let them follow you inside.

questions.question: What should you do?
options: Ask their name and then let them in.
Lend them your badge.
Direct them to the proper check-in or access process.
Hold the door because they seem friendly.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — A believable story does not replace physical access controls.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. A believable story does not replace physical access controls.
questions.explanation: A believable story does not replace physical access controls.

scenario.body: They ask to borrow your logged-in laptop for a 'quick network test.'

questions.question: What is the safest response?
options: Hand over the laptop if they wear a polo shirt.
Tell them your password instead.
Verify their identity and use the approved IT support process.
Let them use it while you watch.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Uniforms, confidence, and technical language can all be part of a pretext.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Uniforms, confidence, and technical language can all be part of a pretext.
questions.explanation: Uniforms, confidence, and technical language can all be part of a pretext.

scenario.body: A student you do not recognize asks for the class group password because 'the teacher forgot to send it.'

questions.question: What should you do?
options: Write it on the classroom board.
Verify with the teacher or group administrator before sharing access information.
Share it because they know the teacher's name.
Post it in the class chat.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Claimed membership should be verified before sharing credentials or access codes.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Claimed membership should be verified before sharing credentials or access codes.
questions.explanation: Claimed membership should be verified before sharing credentials or access codes.

scenario.body: A 'school survey' asks for your birth date, home address, and password.

questions.question: Which requested item is an immediate red flag?
options: Your year level.
Your opinion about classes.
Your favorite subject.
Your password.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Passwords should never be collected through surveys.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Passwords should never be collected through surveys.
questions.explanation: Passwords should never be collected through surveys.

scenario.body: A courier asks to enter a restricted office because the recipient is 'too busy to come out.'

questions.question: What should staff do?
options: Follow the normal delivery and visitor procedure.
Leave the restricted door open.
Let the courier in for convenience.
Give the courier an employee badge.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Attackers may use delivery roles as believable cover stories.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Attackers may use delivery roles as believable cover stories.
questions.explanation: Attackers may use delivery roles as believable cover stories.

scenario.body: Someone claiming to be a school journalist asks for your login to 'verify your student status.'

questions.question: What should you do?
options: Do not provide login credentials and verify the request through the publication's official contact.
Send your password but change it later.
Ask them to promise not to share it.
Send your MFA code instead.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Verification should not require giving another person your credentials.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Verification should not require giving another person your credentials.
questions.explanation: Verification should not require giving another person your credentials.

scenario.body: A person carrying tools asks where the server room is located.

questions.question: What is the safest response?
options: Send them a photo of the door.
Point them there because they have tools.
Walk them there without checking.
Do not disclose restricted-location details unless their need and identity are verified.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Props and job-role stories can be used to gain trust.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Props and job-role stories can be used to gain trust.
questions.explanation: Props and job-role stories can be used to gain trust.

scenario.body: An email from a personal address says HR needs copies of student IDs for an urgent audit.

questions.question: What should you do?
options: Verify the request through the official HR or administration channel.
Reply asking whether a photo is enough.
Send only one ID as a test.
Send the IDs because audits are confidential.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Sensitive-document requests from unexpected channels should be independently verified.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Sensitive-document requests from unexpected channels should be independently verified.
questions.explanation: Sensitive-document requests from unexpected channels should be independently verified.

scenario.body: A visitor says the principal authorized them to inspect every computer and asks you to disable screen locks.

questions.question: What is the best response?
options: Confirm the work order and technician identity with the responsible office.
Let them proceed only on unused computers.
Disable locks because maintenance was authorized.
Ask them to show any business card.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Namedropping an authority figure is not sufficient authorization.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Namedropping an authority figure is not sufficient authorization.
questions.explanation: Namedropping an authority figure is not sufficient authorization.

scenario.body: A new account claiming to be your partner asks for the shared-drive recovery code.

questions.question: What should you do?
options: Send the code because they know the project title.
Contact your partner using the account or method you already know.
Ask the new account for your partner's birthday.
Share only part of the code.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Attackers can build convincing pretexts using information from public or leaked sources.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Attackers can build convincing pretexts using information from public or leaked sources.
questions.explanation: Attackers can build convincing pretexts using information from public or leaked sources.

scenario.body: A caller claims your school's software license expired and needs an administrator username to 'look up the contract.'

questions.question: What is the safest action?
options: Verify the vendor and contract through procurement or IT before sharing anything.
Give only the username because it is not a password.
Install the vendor's tool first.
Give a temporary password.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Even usernames and organizational details can aid later attacks; verify the business relationship first.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Even usernames and organizational details can aid later attacks; verify the business relationship first.
questions.explanation: Even usernames and organizational details can aid later attacks; verify the business relationship first.

scenario.body: Someone calls saying they are a student's parent and urgently need the student's schedule and classroom location.

questions.question: What should staff do?
options: Give only the next class location.
Provide the schedule because the caller knows the student's name.
Ask the caller to name one teacher, then disclose it.
Follow the school's identity-verification and privacy procedure.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Knowledge of basic personal facts does not establish identity or authorization.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Knowledge of basic personal facts does not establish identity or authorization.
questions.explanation: Knowledge of basic personal facts does not establish identity or authorization.

scenario.body: A person claiming to be conducting a cybersecurity study asks you to describe your school's password reset process.

questions.question: Why should you be cautious?
options: Research requests are always illegal.
Password resets never have procedures.
Operational details can help an attacker build a stronger pretext.
Only passwords themselves are sensitive.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Process details can reveal opportunities for social engineering even without exposing credentials.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Process details can reveal opportunities for social engineering even without exposing credentials.
questions.explanation: Process details can reveal opportunities for social engineering even without exposing credentials.

scenario.body: A new assistant says the director authorized an exception and asks you to bypass the normal visitor log.

questions.question: What should you do?
options: Record the visitor after they leave.
Ask for the director's name only.
Bypass it because executive staff have authority.
Follow the established access process unless the exception is independently confirmed.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Pretexting often pressures people to make 'one-time' exceptions to normal controls.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Pretexting often pressures people to make 'one-time' exceptions to normal controls.
questions.explanation: Pretexting often pressures people to make 'one-time' exceptions to normal controls.

scenario.body: A person wearing a school uniform says their badge was stolen and asks to borrow yours for five minutes.

questions.question: What is the safest response?
options: Send them to the office responsible for replacement or temporary credentials.
Swipe them into every door yourself.
Lend the badge if they leave their phone with you.
Give them the badge but keep the lanyard.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Access credentials should not be shared, even when the story seems plausible.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Access credentials should not be shared, even when the story seems plausible.
questions.explanation: Access credentials should not be shared, even when the story seems plausible.

scenario.body: A real employee's messaging account asks for a confidential file that the employee does not normally handle.

questions.question: What is the best response?
options: Verify the unusual request through a separate trusted channel.
Remove the file name and send the contents.
Send it because the account is real.
Ask the same account whether it was hacked.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Behavioral context matters. A real account can be compromised and used for pretexting.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Behavioral context matters. A real account can be compromised and used for pretexting.
questions.explanation: Behavioral context matters. A real account can be compromised and used for pretexting.

scenario.body: A video caller appears to be a manager and asks you to reveal sensitive access information during an emergency.

questions.question: What should you rely on?
options: Ask the caller to wave at the camera.
A manager can override all controls verbally.
Video is impossible to fake convincingly.
Established verification procedures, not appearance or voice alone.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Synthetic audio/video makes visual familiarity insufficient for high-risk requests.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Synthetic audio/video makes visual familiarity insufficient for high-risk requests.
questions.explanation: Synthetic audio/video makes visual familiarity insufficient for high-risk requests.

scenario.body: A person claims to be responding to an active breach and asks you to skip identity checks because 'every second counts.'

questions.question: What should you do?
options: Give them access, then verify afterward.
Share credentials only if they sound technical.
Use the organization's emergency verification procedure and approved contacts.
Skip verification during security emergencies.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Attackers may exploit emergencies to persuade people to bypass controls.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Attackers may exploit emergencies to persuade people to bypass controls.
questions.explanation: Attackers may exploit emergencies to persuade people to bypass controls.

scenario.body: A known supplier's 'new account manager' requests confidential pricing documents and says the old contact left suddenly.

questions.question: What is the safest next step?
options: Trust the new manager because they know the supplier name.
Confirm the personnel change with the supplier using previously established contact information.
Send redacted documents first.
Ask for a LinkedIn profile as proof.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Third-party personnel changes should be verified through a trusted existing relationship.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Third-party personnel changes should be verified through a trusted existing relationship.
questions.explanation: Third-party personnel changes should be verified through a trusted existing relationship.

scenario.body: A convincing form asks which employees have administrator access, what MFA method is used, and who approves password resets.

questions.question: Why can this be sensitive even without asking for passwords?
options: Only IP addresses are sensitive.
It maps people and processes an attacker could target in later social-engineering attempts.
MFA makes this information harmless.
Security processes are never confidential.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Attackers can use organizational process information to choose targets and craft believable stories.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Attackers can use organizational process information to choose targets and craft believable stories.
questions.explanation: Attackers can use organizational process information to choose targets and craft believable stories.

question_types.description: Fast four-choice social-engineering scenarios designed for LevelBlue PvP.

scenario.from: USB drive found in the hallway
scenario.body: The drive is labeled 'FINAL EXAM ANSWERS'.

questions.question: What should you do?
options: Open it on your personal laptop instead.
Give it to the appropriate staff without plugging it into a device.
Ask a friend to test it.
Open it on a school computer.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Curiosity-based baiting often relies on people connecting unknown removable media.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Curiosity-based baiting often relies on people connecting unknown removable media.
questions.explanation: Curiosity-based baiting often relies on people connecting unknown removable media.

scenario.body: A website offers a paid game for free but requires you to disable antivirus first.

questions.question: What is the clearest warning sign?
options: It asks you to weaken security controls before installing.
The file is large.
The site uses dark colors.
The game is popular.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Requests to disable security controls are a major warning sign.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Requests to disable security controls are a major warning sign.
questions.explanation: Requests to disable security controls are a major warning sign.

scenario.body: A poster says 'FREE CAMPUS WIFI - no password' and shows a network name you have never seen.

questions.question: What should you do?
options: Ask another student whether the signal is strong.
Connect because free Wi-Fi is convenient.
Use it only for email.
Confirm the official campus network name before connecting.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Attackers can create lookalike wireless networks to lure users.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Attackers can create lookalike wireless networks to lure users.
questions.explanation: Attackers can create lookalike wireless networks to lure users.

scenario.body: A sticker says 'Scan to win a laptop' and is placed over another QR code.

questions.question: What should you do?
options: Scan it because QR codes cannot be malicious.
Scan it but do not read the page.
Share it with friends first.
Avoid scanning it and use the organization's official site for promotions.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Physical QR stickers can redirect users to attacker-controlled sites.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Physical QR stickers can redirect users to attacker-controlled sites.
questions.explanation: Physical QR stickers can redirect users to attacker-controlled sites.

scenario.body: An unknown kiosk offers free charging and asks you to unlock your phone and select 'Trust this computer.'

questions.question: What is safest?
options: Unlock the phone only once.
Disable the screen lock first.
Do not trust the unknown computer; use a power-only charger or your own adapter.
Trust it because charging requires data access.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Charging should not require granting an unknown computer data access.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Charging should not require granting an unknown computer data access.
questions.explanation: Charging should not require granting an unknown computer data access.

scenario.body: A stranger outside campus hands out USB drives containing 'study tools.'

questions.question: What should you do?
options: Use it only on a library computer.
Format it after opening the files.
Treat unknown removable media as untrusted and do not connect it.
Plug it in without opening anything.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Merely connecting unknown devices can create risk; use approved media.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Merely connecting unknown devices can create risk; use approved media.
questions.explanation: Merely connecting unknown devices can create risk; use approved media.

scenario.body: A pop-up promises a large discount if you enter your school username and password.

questions.question: What is the best response?
options: Enter the password because coupons need verification.
Send the coupon to classmates.
Close it and use the retailer's official site or app.
Use the same password but change it later.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Discounts should not require unrelated school credentials.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Discounts should not require unrelated school credentials.
questions.explanation: Discounts should not require unrelated school credentials.

scenario.body: A download claims to unlock premium editing software and includes a 'patch' executable.

questions.question: Why is this risky?
options: Untrusted cracked software can be used as bait to deliver malware.
Editing software cannot contain malware.
A file is safe if many people downloaded it.
Premium software never uses executables.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Attackers often hide malicious software inside desirable pirated content.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Attackers often hide malicious software inside desirable pirated content.
questions.explanation: Attackers often hide malicious software inside desirable pirated content.

scenario.body: The drive appears to contain salary information.

questions.question: What is the safest handling?
options: Check it on an offline personal computer.
Open it to identify the owner.
Report and turn it over through the organization's approved process without opening it.
Copy the files before returning it.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Sensitive-looking labels are often designed to trigger curiosity.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Sensitive-looking labels are often designed to trigger curiosity.
questions.explanation: Sensitive-looking labels are often designed to trigger curiosity.

scenario.body: A site promises perfect answers if you upload your school account session file or browser cookies.

questions.question: What should you do?
options: Do not upload session data; use approved tools without sharing authentication material.
Upload them and log out afterward.
Upload only cookies from the school site.
Send the files to a friend to test.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Session tokens and cookies can grant account access without a password.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Session tokens and cookies can grant account access without a password.
questions.explanation: Session tokens and cookies can grant account access without a password.

scenario.body: A booth offers headphones if you install an unknown mobile app and grant accessibility permissions.

questions.question: What is the safest response?
options: Use a friend's phone.
Install it, claim the prize, then uninstall.
Grant permissions only for five minutes.
Do not grant powerful permissions to an unverified app for a reward.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Rewards can be used to convince users to grant dangerous permissions.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Rewards can be used to convince users to grant dangerous permissions.
questions.explanation: Rewards can be used to convince users to grant dangerous permissions.

scenario.body: A message offers a normally expensive textbook for free from an unfamiliar download site.

questions.question: What should you check?
options: Whether the filename includes the book title.
Use legitimate library or publisher sources instead of downloading from an untrusted site.
Whether the page has five-star reviews.
Whether the file is a PDF.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — A desirable file type or convincing reviews do not make an unknown source safe.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. A desirable file type or convincing reviews do not make an unknown source safe.
questions.explanation: A desirable file type or convincing reviews do not make an unknown source safe.

scenario.body: A promotional cable from an unknown source includes unexpected data-transfer behavior when connected.

questions.question: What is the security lesson?
options: A cable is safe if it charges normally.
Cables cannot affect security.
Only wireless devices can be malicious.
Treat unknown hardware accessories as potentially untrusted, not just unknown files.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Hardware itself can be part of a baiting attack.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Hardware itself can be part of a baiting attack.
questions.explanation: Hardware itself can be part of a baiting attack.

scenario.body: A streaming site says, 'Your video player is outdated—download this update to continue.'

questions.question: What is the safest action?
options: Install the offered update because the video requires it.
Disable browser protection first.
Update software through the official app store or vendor site instead.
Download it but rename the file.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Unexpected update prompts on unrelated sites can be bait for malicious downloads.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Unexpected update prompts on unrelated sites can be bait for malicious downloads.
questions.explanation: Unexpected update prompts on unrelated sites can be bait for malicious downloads.

scenario.body: A site offers 1 TB of free storage if you 'connect' your school account and approve broad permissions.

questions.question: What should you do?
options: Approve because OAuth means no password is shared.
Grant access only during school hours.
Review the service and permissions through approved channels before granting access.
Approve and revoke it later if something happens.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — OAuth permissions can expose data even when you never type your password into the third-party site.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. OAuth permissions can expose data even when you never type your password into the third-party site.
questions.explanation: OAuth permissions can expose data even when you never type your password into the third-party site.

scenario.body: A branded USB drive is handed out at an event by someone wearing the event logo.

questions.question: Why should you still use caution?
options: Event merchandise is always screened.
Logos provide cryptographic verification.
Branding and physical appearance do not prove the device came from a trusted source.
USB devices cannot impersonate other hardware.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Physical branding can be copied; unknown devices still require approved handling.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Physical branding can be copied; unknown devices still require approved handling.
questions.explanation: Physical branding can be copied; unknown devices still require approved handling.

scenario.body: A new sticker has been placed over the poster's printed QR code.

questions.question: What is the best response?
options: Photograph the QR code and scan it later.
Do not scan it; report the altered poster and navigate to the official site manually.
Scan the sticker because it is newer.
Scan both codes and compare them.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — QR-code replacement is a physical baiting technique that redirects users to malicious destinations.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. QR-code replacement is a physical baiting technique that redirects users to malicious destinations.
questions.explanation: QR-code replacement is a physical baiting technique that redirects users to malicious destinations.

scenario.body: An extension promises exam-answer summaries but requests permission to read and change data on every website you visit.

questions.question: What is the key concern?
options: Browser extensions cannot access websites.
A high rating guarantees safety.
Permissions only matter on mobile devices.
The requested permissions are excessive for the claimed function.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Permission scope should match the tool's purpose; excessive access creates unnecessary risk.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Permission scope should match the tool's purpose; excessive access creates unnecessary risk.
questions.explanation: Permission scope should match the tool's purpose; excessive access creates unnecessary risk.

scenario.body: A stranger offers cash if you install a 'school security testing agent' and send them the activation code.

questions.question: What should you do?
options: Install it on a shared computer instead.
Install it because security testing is beneficial.
Ask for more money first.
Refuse and verify any security-testing activity through authorized school staff.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — A claimed security purpose does not make unauthorized software safe.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. A claimed security purpose does not make unauthorized software safe.
questions.explanation: A claimed security purpose does not make unauthorized software safe.

scenario.body: A convincing invite from a popular service asks you to sideload an app profile that grants device-management control.

questions.question: What is the safest response?
options: Grant control temporarily.
Use the service's official distribution channel and do not grant device-management control to an unverified profile.
Install it because beta software often needs extra permissions.
Use a spare account but the same phone.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — Device-management profiles can provide extensive control and should come only from trusted, authorized sources.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Not quite. Device-management profiles can provide extensive control and should come only from trusted, authorized sources.
questions.explanation: Device-management profiles can provide extensive control and should come only from trusted, authorized sources.
